To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) income and education are both associated with inflammation; (2) the effect of income on inflammation is stronger than education; (3) the effect of education is stronger for MAs and NHBs compared to NHWs; and (4) the effect of educational attainment on inflammation is stronger for intermediate and high CRPs compared to low CRPs for all race/ethnic groups.
education is a better predictor of elevated CRPs in race/ethnic groups compared to income.

educational attainment is a strong predictor of inflammation in race/ethnic groups in the United States and that MAs have a unique pattern of inflammation by educational attainment compared to NHWs and NHBs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of education on inflammation in a nationally representative sample of the U.S. population.
understanding the role of SES in explaining race/ethnic differences in inflammatory risk and the biological mechanisms by which SES “get under the skin.”
the impact of education and income on observed race/ethnic disparities in inflammation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
educational attainment is a better indicator of SES than income in explaining the higher inflammation burden among race/ethnic populations.
the association between race and ethnicity and elevated inflammation is mediated by educational attainment.

educational attainment, rather than income, is a stronger predictor of elevated inflammation levels and may be a key pathway in the explanation of observed disparities in cardiovascular disease for NHBs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
educational attainment has a strong influence on the observed racial/ethnic disparities in inflammation and that this influence is not fully explained by other traditional CVD risk factors.
educational attainment is a more important SES predictor of inflammation than income and that MAs have greater vulnerability to elevated inflammation levels than NHBs.

educational attainment may be a more powerful predictor of inflammation in NHBs and certain Hispanic sub-groups than income and may be a better predictor for the SES-inflammations pathway in race/ethnic groups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
educational attainment is a strong predictor of inflammation in the U.S. and may be more powerful in explaining race/ethnic disparities in inflammation than income.

educational attainment is a better predictor of CRP in race/ethnic minority groups compared to income and that educational attainment should be considered in future studies of the SES-inflammations pathway.

education is a more powerful predictor than income of inflammation burden in race/ethnic groups and that MAs may be more susceptible to the adverse effects of low education attainment on elevated CRP levels compared NHBs.
